title: Chennai Leather & Footwear: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Chennai's leather and footwear units tan hides, cut and stitch uppers, and assemble shoes, turning hides, chemicals and components into finished goods sold to exporters and domestic brands.** Tamil Nadu and Kerala together contribute around 38 per cent of India's total output and over 45 per cent of its exports [1], so this city sits inside the country's densest leather cluster. Cash arrives from two very different buyers: export orders priced in dollars and domestic brand orders on credit. **The export leg is the fragile one right now** — India's footwear, leather and leather products exports were around 4.83 billion US dollars last year [1], and India-wide exports are down 3.0 per cent Apr-to-date in USD [D].

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in the tanning and finishing stage, not in stitching**, because effluent treatment and chemical costs are fixed while cutting and stitching can be outsourced [11]. Rating work flags that effluent and pollution compliance carries real additional cost [10], so a tannery's licence is an asset and a liability at once. Working capital is hide inventory plus export receivables; capex is plant, machinery and retail reach [8]. **Peer numbers show the margin squeeze**: the listed leather basket runs a net profit margin of 6.65 per cent with quarterly profit down 4.79 per cent YoY [5], and Leiner Shoes saw operating income fall from 261.27 crore to 221.35 crore and PBILDT from 28.13 crore to 18.69 crore between March 2025 and March 2026 [9].

## What has changed now
**The local demand signal is weak.** Tamil Nadu GST collections are down 3.2 per cent Apr-to-date against India's plus 6.1 per cent, 9.3 percentage points slower [D], and repo has moved to 5.5 per cent with a tightening stance [D]. Against that, IIP for leather-linked output is plus 8.1 per cent YoY [D] — production is running ahead of collections, which usually means inventory is building somewhere in the chain. **The positive is structural, not immediate**: the India-EU free trade agreement is expected to cut tariffs on leather goods [1], and a CSIR-CLRI design studio has opened for the sector [2]. A June 2026 Chennai consultation on sector growth [3] confirms policy attention but gives no numbers. Note the fair report [1] is dated February 2026 and the peer pieces [4][6][7] are old or undated — treat them as background, not current trading.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue tier-2 suppliers to organised brands and export houses with own effluent treatment, low gearing and domestic order books** — Leiner's overall gearing of 0.09x [9] shows what a clean balance sheet looks like in this trade. Avoid pure export converters with no forward cover, and avoid units whose pollution consent is pending. When a proposal lands, check the effluent consent validity and the buyer-wise order book first; if export receivables exceed domestic, ask for the forward cover and the buyer's payment history. Structure as a cash-flow loan against receivables with a drawing power linked to realised export proceeds, not to invoices raised. Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, quarterly GST returns matched to sales, and the pollution board consent renewal date every year.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch inventory days and receivable days together** — if both stretch while GST filings stay flat, the unit is funding unsold stock. If a borrower's Tamil Nadu GST payment falls for two straight months while sales invoices rise, ask for the purchase register. If export realisations slip below the invoiced dollar value, check the forward book before renewing the limit.
